thread.title: West Virginia bluegrass: Family, tradition and the music in their blood
thread.title_full: West Virginia bluegrass: Family, tradition and the music in their blood

author: Faithlyn Graham STAFF WRITER
title: West Virginia bluegrass: Family, tradition and the music in their blood
text:
CLARKSBURG W.Va. (WV News) — Bluegrass music may have been named in Kentucky, but its roots run deep in West Virginia.
From coal camps to mountain festivals, the state has produced its share of pickers, fiddlers and singers whose sounds helped shape the genre.
More than music
As John Arnold of the Hampshire County bluegrass band One Lane Road said, before there were phones or the internet, there was music.
“(People) played music on the porch on Saturday nights and maybe a square dance,” said Arnold, a seasoned banjoist. “Music is kind of, to me, in the blood of West Virginians.”
Even today, though bluegrass has declined in popularity, it continues to thrive in West Virginia through traditions passed between generations. Almost every musician in the state’s bluegrass scene started by following in their family’s footsteps.
One Lane Road, for example, is almost entirely made up of relatives: Arnold, his great-nephews Lane and Kade Suddath, their father, Luke Suddath, and Carson Saffle, a close family friend.
“Growing up with my brother playing music and my dad playing some music, I’ve always craved playing music in a band setting with my kids,” Luke Suddath said. “I’ve had more fun and it’s more exciting to me playing music now than it ever has been.”
It’s not only a way to bring families closer together but also a way to build community.
“It’s expanded my social circle dramatically,” said Cary Landis, a banjo and guitar player. “It gives me a way to make an instant friend. Even if I go out of town, I can find a bluegrass jam and meet somebody.”
Landis plays with an unofficial band called Wayfair Bluegrass. Wayfair has a few core members, but the lineup changes depending on who wants to play.
Building a culture
Landis said jam sessions are central to bluegrass culture because they bring musicians together. He prefers to call what he does an “organized jam” rather than an “open jam,” which he describes as more structured than the average session.
That’s because in “open jams,” unspoken etiquette is sometimes broken, which can make the experience less enjoyable. Bluegrass jam etiquette centers on respecting tradition and sharing the music.
Each player takes turns leading songs, with the leader choosing the tune, directing solos and signaling when the song will end, often with a subtle gesture. Songs typically run about three verses to keep them moving smoothly. Players are expected to stay in time and in tune, and beginners are encouraged not to play too loudly. Musicians are expected to call familiar, traditional bluegrass tunes rather than long “jam busters” or personal originals, and to bring only standard bluegrass instruments.
At its heart, jam etiquette is about making space for everyone, keeping the music enjoyable and honoring tradition.
Traditions like these help keep bluegrass culture in West Virginia and the Appalachian region alive and thriving.
Taking breaks from bluegrass
Both Arnold and Landis took pauses in their bluegrass careers — something they say is common for musicians.
“It’s pretty common to get out of high school or get out of college, get busy, and not even realize it was important — that it was a part of my identity rather than just a fun thing that I was doing,” Landis said. “I’d say it’s the same reason people get out of high school, stop playing baseball, or just get busy.”
Though Landis stepped away early in his career, Arnold took a break later in life after a successful run with the regional band Lonesome Highway.
“I think for me it kind of runs its course a little bit, and we’re just kind of like, ‘I think I’m done doing this for a while,’” Arnold said. “We’d leave on Fridays a lot of times and I wouldn’t get back till Sunday. It was fun and all, and we made a little money, but not enough to sustain a living doing it. Everybody had to have other jobs.”
Despite these pauses, both returned to the West Virginia bluegrass scene — proof, as Arnold put it, that the music is in their blood.
